text: What name should appear on your résumé?
why: Use the professional name you want employers to see.

text: Which email can employers use to contact you?
why: A reliable contact method is part of a usable résumé.

text: What are you looking for next?
why: Your target determines which real experiences to emphasize.

text: Where are you in your studies?
why: A first-year student should get prompts about labs and projects, even with no employment.

text: Where do you study?
why: Your school provides context for your education.

text: What degree and major are you working toward?
why: State the degree accurately, including a minor if relevant.

text: When do you expect to graduate?
why: Expected graduation helps recruiters assess internship timing.

text: Have you had a job, internship, or paid responsibility?
why: Work outside your major can still demonstrate useful skills.

text: Which of these have you tried?
why: Small responsibilities can contain strong evidence. Choose anything that applies.

text: Tell me about one thing you did that someone relied on.
why: Start with a real event. It does not need to have been a job.
example: I helped our club keep track of expenses in a spreadsheet.

text: Would you like to include a phone number?
why: Optional. Include a number you are comfortable sharing with employers.

text: What city or region are you based in?
why: City and region are sufficient; your street address is unnecessary.

text: What is your LinkedIn URL?
why: Link to a profile you have reviewed.

text: What is your GitHub URL?
why: Repositories can give recruiters concrete examples of your work.

text: Do you have a portfolio or personal website?
why: A working project link can help demonstrate what you built.

text: Would you like to include your GPA and its scale?
why: Optional: keep the exact value and scale from your school.

text: Which classes have given you skills relevant to your target?
why: Choose a few relevant courses; distinguish current from completed courses.

text: Have you earned honors, scholarships, or academic awards?
why: Include the award name, issuer, and date; do not infer membership from GPA.

text: What is one lab or class assignment you can explain and demonstrate?
why: A first-year résumé can begin with classroom evidence.

text: Have you worked with a professor or research group?
why: Explain your actual role, methods, and any permitted public output.

text: Which kinds of problems make you curious?
why: Interests and demonstrated abilities are separate signals.

text: What work arrangement would you prefer?
why: A preference guides exploration and does not establish job eligibility.

text: What kind of opportunity do you want?
why: Distinguishes an internship search from full-time exploration.

text: Where would you like to work, and could you relocate?
why: Location can affect whether an opportunity is practical.

text: Are there industries or organizations you are interested in?
why: A sector can shape which domain knowledge matters.

text: Which project or class have you enjoyed most, and why?
why: Specific tasks are more useful than a personality label.

text: How would you like to spend most of your working day?
why: Work preferences help you compare daily responsibilities.

text: Would you rather analyze an open-ended problem or build a concrete solution?
why: Neither preference is better. Explain with an example.

text: What have you tried so far, and what would you like to try next?
why: Exploration recommendations should be small experiments, not definitive judgments.

text: Do you have a job description you want to use?
why: Paste it in Job match to compare stated requirements with your evidence.

text: Which technical tools or languages have you used?
why: These begin as self-reported skills until linked to an example.

text: Pick one skill. What did you actually do with it, and where?
why: An example is more meaningful than an arbitrary 1–10 rating.

text: When did you last use those skills, and what could you do independently?
why: Recency and independence support an honest discussion of capability.

text: Which languages can you communicate in, and in what contexts?
why: Only include proficiency you can accurately describe.

text: Have you earned any certifications?
why: List issuer, credential name, completion date, and optional verification link. Mark in-progress credentials clearly.

text: How could someone inspect or reproduce your work?
why: A repository, test, demonstration, or artifact is stronger than a self-rating.

text: What is in your existing résumé that we have not captured?
why: Imported text is unverified until you confirm each fact. Use Import in your profile.

text: How would you describe this experience in your own words?
why: A rough description is enough to begin. We will uncover the specifics together.

text: What problem or need were you working on?
why: Context helps explain why your contribution mattered.

text: What did you personally do?
why: Separate your own contribution from the overall team result.

text: What tools, technologies, or methods did you actually use?
why: Links concrete work to skills; a mention is not an expert rating.

text: What happened as a result of your work?
why: A qualitative result is useful when there is no reliable number.

text: Is there a number or range you can honestly support?
why: Include the unit and time period. A confirmed estimate or no number is fine.
example: For example: about 8–12 customers per shift, based on the daily log.

text: Who did you work with, and what was your role?
why: Distinguishes collaboration, support, and ownership.

text: What was the hardest part, and how did you solve it?
why: Shows the thinking behind the task.

text: When did you explain your work to someone else?
why: Communication should be shown through a concrete situation.

text: What did you learn or become able to do independently?
why: Helps distinguish emerging skills from demonstrated independence.

text: Is there a public link or artifact you can share?
why: Only share work you have permission to disclose.

text: Is there a public link or artifact you can share?
why: Only share work you have permission to disclose.

text: Which devices and hardware or software problems did you diagnose?
why: Repair work can demonstrate systematic troubleshooting.

text: Did you recover data or handle sensitive information? What precautions did you take?
why: Describe approved methods without exposing customer data.

text: What did you help customers understand or decide?
why: Specific customer situations provide communication evidence.

text: Did you automate or simplify any repetitive task?
why: Capture the original process and what you changed.

text: Were you responsible for opening, closing, inventory, or working independently?
why: Operational responsibility can demonstrate reliability.

text: Did you train someone? What did you teach and how?
why: Training can provide leadership evidence without inflating your title.

text: Did your work change turnaround time, errors, cost, or reliability?
why: Ask for a baseline before describing an improvement.

text: How often did you perform this work?
why: Frequency gives scope even when there is no formal impact metric.

text: How did the main parts of your project fit together?
why: Shows understanding beyond listing a technology stack.

text: What did you implement in the user interface?
why: Identify your own design or frontend contribution.

text: What happened on the server, and what did you implement?
why: Distinguishes an API integration from building a backend.

text: How did you structure, query, or validate the data?
why: Database decisions can provide concrete technical evidence.

text: How did you test it, and what failure did a test catch?
why: Specific verification is stronger than saying it was reliable.

text: What permissions, authentication, or security risks did you address?
why: Name controls you implemented and verified.

text: Where did you deploy it, and what did you manage yourself?
why: A local prototype and a deployed service are different claims.

text: Did you measure speed, resource use, or reliability?
why: State the test conditions and baseline; do not imply unmeasured gains.

text: Where did your data come from, and how did you check its quality?
why: Data provenance and leakage prevention matter in data and AI projects.

text: How did you evaluate the model or analysis, and against what baseline?
why: Avoid unsupported accuracy claims and test-set leakage.

text: What system were you allowed to assess, and what did you find?
why: Security experience needs clear scope, permission, and remediation.

text: Which design tradeoff or code review changed your implementation?
why: Software engineering includes technical judgment and collaboration.

text: How did you monitor or debug the system when something failed?
why: Systems work is demonstrated through operation and diagnosis.

text: How did you design, measure, or test the physical system?
why: Hardware claims need test conditions and your exact contribution.

text: What decision or responsibility did you personally own?
why: Leadership is an action, not just a club membership.

text: Did you organize an event? What did you coordinate?
why: Capture the purpose, logistics, and confirmed scope.

text: How did you help someone understand a difficult topic?
why: Tutoring can demonstrate communication and subject knowledge.

text: Did you maintain content, a community, or a shared service?
why: Record actual responsibilities and a confirmed audience size if known.

text: Was your work recognized, published, or awarded?
why: Record the issuer, date, title, and your contribution.

text: Which relevant courses did you complete here?
why: Keep current and completed classes distinguishable.

text: Which honors or scholarships did you receive here?
why: Record the exact name and date.
